summary: Describes a system deployed by the ISP Comcast to deliver critical notifications to customers' web browsers, for example warning that their traffic looks like malware infection. It documents one provider's design and its status is historic.

eli5.summary: An internet company wanted a way to pop up a warning on your web browser, like a note on your door, if your computer seemed to be sick.

questions: how can an isp warn customers about malware in the browser
how does comcast notify customers of malware
subtitle: How an ISP warns customers about malware through their web browser.

tldr.problem: Internet Service Providers need a way to notify customers if their network traffic suggests malware infection, but many existing solutions use invasive Deep Packet Inspection technology.
tldr.mechanism: Comcast documented a system using open standards: traffic is routed through a web proxy, which asks an ICAP server to insert a notification message into web pages when the customer needs to be warned.
tldr.outcome: The system was deployed but is now historic as network management practices evolved. The approach showed that open standards could provide an alternative to DPI.

today: RFC 6108 is Historic. It describes a system Comcast deployed to provide critical notifications to customers' web browsers. The RFC documents the design for reference, though the system's use and evolution in actual networks is beyond what the document states.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Internet Service Providers need a way to notify customers if their network traffic shows signs of malware infection, such as unusual connection patterns. Rather than use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI), which examines the content of every packet in detail, Comcast designed a system based on open protocols. The system identifies customers who need warnings and delivers notifications through their web browsers using existing IETF standards.

The RFC documents the system Comcast deployed: it uses a web proxy server, an ICAP server to adapt web content, and a messaging service to cache notifications. The authors emphasize that the system was designed to avoid the privacy concerns of DPI while still reaching customers when they browse the web.
sections.eli5: Instead of watching everything you download, the internet company used normal web tools to pop up a warning on your browser, kind of like a sticky note on your computer screen.

sections.title: How the System Works
sections.content:
The web notification system has five main components: a web proxy (Squid), an ICAP server (GreasySpoon), a customer database, a messaging service (Apache Tomcat), and a Session Management Broker that directs traffic. When a customer who needs a notification makes an HTTP request, the Session Management Broker routes their traffic to the web proxy. The proxy fetches the web page and sends it to the ICAP server, which checks whether a notification should be inserted. If the messaging service has a cached notification for that customer's IP address, the ICAP server inserts it into the HTTP response. The modified page is sent back to the customer's browser.

A key requirement was that the system must handle existing TCP port 80 sessions gracefully: if a customer already has a connection open when they are identified as needing a notification, that connection must not be interrupted. The system uses differentiated services (Diffserv) to mark packets that need the notification treatment.
sections.eli5: A load balancer sits at the door and picks out traffic from customers who need a warning. It sends that traffic through the proxy layer, which asks the ICAP server to add a warning message to web pages.

sections.title: Design Constraints and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC lists 12 general requirements that shaped the design. The system must only show critical notifications, use port 80 (HTTP), and support a block list of websites where the notification might cause problems. It must not disrupt instant messaging or other non-HTTP traffic on port 80, and must handle active TCP sessions without interruption. TCP resets are not allowed. User notification acknowledgement must immediately stop further notifications so customers know their action was recognized.

Additional requirements ensure the system does not modify content it should not touch, handles unexpected content gracefully, avoids caching user data, and never inserts or replaces advertising. The RFC emphasizes that the system was designed to be transparent and limited in scope, addressing legitimate security notification needs without the collateral damage of older DPI-based systems.
sections.eli5: The system had to be polite: only showing real warnings, not breaking other programs, stopping when you said yes, and never changing ads on websites.

sections.title: Message Flow and User Experience
sections.content:
When a notification is needed, the system follows a precise flow. The Session Management Broker routes the customer's HTTP request to the web proxy. The proxy forwards it to the destination website and receives the response. The proxy then sends the response to the ICAP server with a request to adapt it. The ICAP server queries the Messaging Service, which checks its cache for a notification for that customer's IP address. If a match is found, the ICAP server inserts the notification message into the HTTP response body without altering the original website content. If no notification is cached, the ICAP server returns a 204 (No Content) response, and the original page is sent unchanged.

The notification displayed to the user is an HTML/JavaScript overlay that warns of malware infection and may direct them to a remediation page. The user can acknowledge, snooze, or request more information. Once acknowledged, the notification is removed from the Messaging Service cache and future requests do not receive it.
sections.eli5: When your page loads, the system checks if a warning is waiting for you. If yes, it adds it to the page. If you click OK, the warning stops appearing. Simple.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC devotes a section to security considerations and potential concerns. Because a notification warns of malware, users might mistake it for a phishing attack; the text and visual design are therefore carefully chosen. The notification never asks for login credentials or a password change, which are common phishing tactics. To help users verify the warning is legitimate, customer support can confirm that a notification was sent. The RFC also discusses why such a system was considered necessary: host-based malware defense was often insufficient, and ISPs were being urged by governments and security organizations to take action against the scale of malware infection.

The authors also address the debate over whether it is appropriate for ISPs to modify content at all, even for security notifications. They argue that the open-standards approach is preferable to widespread DPI deployment and that transparent disclosure serves the Internet community better than silent network management.
sections.eli5: The warning is real and helpful, not a trick. If you call customer service, they can tell you that yes, we sent you that warning today.
